## Checking a file from elsewhere

`checkRedaction` from `@inkbar/engine` reports what it finds under redactions in any PDF. Without `regions`, it looks for candidates itself: Redact annotations, filled boxes in the page content, and Square, Highlight and Stamp annotations drawn as one opaque filled box. That is the use for a file Inkbar did not just produce.

A crafted file can make the check take a long time, so run it on an engine of its own, in its own worker (the default in a browser), with a timeout, and destroy that engine when the timeout fires:

```ts
import { createEngine } from '@inkbar/engine'


const engine = await createEngine()
const timeout = setTimeout(() => void engine.destroy(), 30_000)
try {
  const { candidates, file } = await engine.checkRedaction(bytes)
  const flagged = candidates.filter((candidate) => candidate.verdict !== 'clean')
} finally {
  clearTimeout(timeout)
  await engine.destroy()
}
```

Each candidate gives its `page` and `rect`, its `kind`, whether `text`, `image` or `drawing` is present under it, and a `verdict`: `unapplied` for a Redact annotation with anything under it, `content-remains` for any other candidate with anything under it, and `clean` when the check found nothing under it. `file` counts the earlier versions and attached files the file keeps, and says whether it has metadata, scripts, hidden layers or a digital signature. Findings never hold text from the file.

`clean` means the check found nothing under that place. Without `regions`, the check reports only the redactions it recognises, and a filled box with nothing under it is `clean` whether it is a redaction or a graphic. A `check-failed` error means the check could not inspect a page or the file: treat it as a failed check, never as a finding of nothing. The [`@inkbar/engine` README](https://github.com/inkbar/inkbar/tree/main/packages/engine#checking-a-redaction) has the rules, the thresholds and the full list of limits.

# Controlled mode

> Hold the annotation list in your own state and let Inkbar propose each change.

By default Inkbar holds the annotations itself and gives you undo and redo. In controlled mode your app holds the list, and Inkbar proposes each change to you. Use it when the annotations belong in your own store, for example to save them as they change or to sync them between people.

Annotations embedded in the PDF stay inside Inkbar and never appear in your list.

In the examples, `loadAnnotations` stands for your own call to your server.

* Vue

  With `v-model:annotations`, Inkbar proposes each change through `update:annotations` and shows whatever list you pass back. To change annotations yourself, replace the array: `annotations.value = [...annotations.value, next]`. In-place mutation (`push`, `splice`, editing an item) is not observed, so the viewer never sees it.

  Undo and redo are off in controlled mode unless you pass `:history="true"`. Inkbar then keeps a stack of your list’s past values and applies undo and redo through `v-model`. Every change to the list is a step, including the list you load from your server when the document opens. Clear the history once that load has reached the viewer, so the first undo does not empty the list:

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { nextTick, ref, useTemplateRef } from 'vue'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/vue'
  import type { Annotation, InkDocument } from '@inkbar/core'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  defineProps<{ signedUrl: string; documentId: string }>()


  const annotations = ref<Annotation[]>([])
  const root = useTemplateRef<InstanceType<typeof InkRoot>>('root')


  async function onReady(doc: InkDocument) {
    annotations.value = await loadAnnotations(doc.key)
    await nextTick()
    root.value?.history.clear()
  }
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot
      ref="root"
      v-model:annotations="annotations"
      :history="true"
      :src="{ url: signedUrl, key: documentId }"
      :assets="assets"
      @ready="onReady"
    >
      <InkViewport />
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

  Inside `InkRoot`, `useHistory()` returns the same object.

  `key` identifies the document. Reuse the same key when only the signed URL changes and the document is not reloaded.

* React

  With `annotations` and `onAnnotationsChange`, Inkbar proposes each change through `onAnnotationsChange` and shows whatever list you pass back. To change annotations yourself, set a new array: `setAnnotations([...annotations, next])`. In-place mutation (`push`, `splice`, editing an item) is not observed, so the viewer never sees it.

  Undo and redo are off in controlled mode unless you pass `history`. Inkbar then keeps a stack of your list’s past values and applies undo and redo through `onAnnotationsChange`. Every change to the list is a step, including the list you load from your server when the document opens. Clear the history once that load has reached the viewer, so the first undo does not empty the list:

  ```tsx
  import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/react'
  import type { InkRootHandle } from '@inkbar/react'
  import type { Annotation, InkDocument } from '@inkbar/core'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  export function Review({
    signedUrl,
    documentId,
  }: {
    signedUrl: string
    documentId: string
  }) {
    const [annotations, setAnnotations] = useState<Annotation[]>([])
    const [loaded, setLoaded] = useState<string | null>(null)
    const root = useRef<InkRootHandle>(null)


    async function onReady(doc: InkDocument) {
      setAnnotations(await loadAnnotations(doc.key))
      setLoaded(doc.key)
    }


    // Runs after InkRoot has seen the loaded list.
    useEffect(() => {
      if (loaded) root.current?.history.clear()
    }, [loaded])


    return (
      <InkRoot
        ref={root}
        annotations={annotations}
        onAnnotationsChange={setAnnotations}
        history
        src={{ url: signedUrl, key: documentId }}
        assets={assets}
        onReady={onReady}
      >
        <InkViewport />
      </InkRoot>
    )
  }
  ```

  Inside `InkRoot`, `useHistory()` returns the same object.

  `key` identifies the document. Reuse the same key when only the signed URL changes and the document is not reloaded.

* Svelte

  With `bind:annotations`, Inkbar proposes each change by writing the binding and shows whatever list it holds. To change annotations yourself, replace the array: `annotations = [...annotations, next]`. In-place mutation (`push`, `splice`, editing an item) is not observed, so the viewer never sees it. Declare the list with `$state.raw`, since Inkbar replaces it whole.

  To decide on each proposal before it applies, use a function binding. The setter receives the proposed list; apply it, change it or drop it:

  ```svelte
  <InkRoot
    src={{ url: signedUrl, key: documentId }}
    {assets}
    bind:annotations={() => annotations, (next) => (annotations = next.filter(allowed))}
  >
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

  Undo and redo are off in controlled mode unless you pass `history={true}`. Inkbar then keeps a stack of your list’s past values and applies undo and redo through the binding. Every change to the list is a step, including the list you load from your server when the document opens. Clear the history once that load has reached the viewer, so the first undo does not empty the list:

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import { tick } from 'svelte'
    import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import type { InkRootHandle } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import type { Annotation, InkDocument } from '@inkbar/core'
    import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


    let { signedUrl, documentId }: { signedUrl: string; documentId: string } = $props()


    let annotations = $state.raw<Annotation[]>([])
    let root = $state<InkRootHandle | undefined>()


    async function onReady(doc: InkDocument) {
      annotations = await loadAnnotations(doc.key)
      await tick()
      root?.history.clear()
    }
  </script>


  <InkRoot
    bind:this={root}
    bind:annotations
    history={true}
    src={{ url: signedUrl, key: documentId }}
    {assets}
    {onReady}
  >
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

  Inside `InkRoot`, `useHistory()` returns the same object.

  `key` identifies the document. Reuse the same key when only the signed URL changes and the document is not reloaded.

## Without a framework

Pass `annotations: { mode: 'controlled', initial, onChange }` to [`createViewer`](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/frameworks/plain-dom/#the-whole-viewer). `onChange` hears each proposed list, and nothing shows until you push a list back with `viewer.document.get()?.annotations.setControlledValue(next)`. `initial` applies to every document the viewer opens, including after `viewer.open()`, so push your own list in `onReady` for each new document:

```ts
import type { Annotation } from '@inkbar/core'
import { createViewer } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


let annotations: Annotation[] = []


const viewer = createViewer(el, {
  source: { url: signedUrl, key: documentId },
  assets,
  annotations: {
    mode: 'controlled',
    initial: [],
    onChange: (next) => {
      annotations = next
      viewer.document.get()?.annotations.setControlledValue(next)
    },
  },
  onReady: async (doc) => {
    annotations = await loadAnnotations(doc.key)
    doc.annotations.setControlledValue(annotations)
  },
})
```

To refuse a change, leave it out of the list you push back. Undo and redo do nothing in controlled mode: your app owns the list, so it owns undo too.

## Files Inkbar saved

When a file holds annotations that Inkbar [saved into it](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/saving/#opening-a-saved-file), Inkbar proposes them once after the document opens: your list with the saved annotations added, with the reason `'file'`. Apply that proposal as you apply any other. Until your list holds them, the viewer does not show them, and each save still keeps them in the file.

## Form fields

Form field values work the same way. Pass `fields` (`v-model:fields` in Vue, `bind:fields` in Svelte) to hold them in your own state. Inkbar keeps no undo history for controlled fields, and fields join the annotation history only when both are uncontrolled. [Forms](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/forms/#controlled-fields) has the examples.

# Plugins

> Add a plugin to a viewer, place its commands and tools, load and save its records, and share undo with annotations.

A plugin adds features to a viewer without changing Inkbar. It can bring:

* commands, actions with a label that you place as buttons
* tools, which you place with a tool button like the built-in ones
* decorations on annotation elements
* page layers, drawn over every page above the annotations, such as marks that open a card
* record stores, a list of its own records for each open document

A plugin is written once with `definePlugin` from `@inkbar/core/dom` and runs in every framework package and in `createViewer`. Everything it adds is named under its id: command `suggest` of plugin `review` is `review.suggest`. This page is for the app that uses a plugin. To build one, see [Writing a plugin](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/writing-a-plugin/).

## Adding a plugin

Call a factory-style plugin with its options, and pass a plugin written as an object as it is; the plugin’s docs say which. Pass the result to `InkRoot` as `plugins`, or to `createViewer`. The list is read once, when the root mounts: a later change to it is not applied, so make the plugins once rather than on every render.

Nothing a plugin registers shows by itself. Place each command with `InkCommand` and each tool with `InkToolButton`, inside an `InkToolbar`, as you place the built-in controls. A plugin’s tools join the viewer’s on their own, so `tools` lists only the built-in tools you offer:

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { InkCommand, InkRoot, InkToolbar, InkToolButton, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/vue'
  import { redactAreaTool } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  import { review } from './review-plugin'


  defineProps<{ file: File }>()


  const tools = [redactAreaTool()]
  const plugins = [review()]
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot :src="file" :assets="assets" :tools="tools" :plugins="plugins">
      <InkToolbar>
        <InkToolButton tool="redact-area" />
        <InkToolButton tool="review.stamp" />
        <InkCommand id="review.suggest" />
      </InkToolbar>
      <InkViewport />
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import {
    InkCommand,
    InkRoot,
    InkToolbar,
    InkToolButton,
    InkViewport,
  } from '@inkbar/react'
  import { redactAreaTool } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  import { review } from './review-plugin'


  const tools = [redactAreaTool()]
  const plugins = [review()]


  export function Review({ file }: { file: File }) {
    return (
      <InkRoot src={file} assets={assets} tools={tools} plugins={plugins}>
        <InkToolbar>
          <InkToolButton tool="redact-area" />
          <InkToolButton tool="review.stamp" />
          <InkCommand id="review.suggest" />
        </InkToolbar>
        <InkViewport />
      </InkRoot>
    )
  }
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import {
      InkCommand,
      InkRoot,
      InkToolbar,
      InkToolButton,
      InkViewport,
    } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import { redactAreaTool } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
    import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


    import { review } from './review-plugin'


    let { file }: { file: File } = $props()


    const tools = [redactAreaTool()]
    const plugins = [review()]
  </script>


  <InkRoot src={file} {assets} {tools} {plugins}>
    <InkToolbar>
      <InkToolButton tool="redact-area" />
      <InkToolButton tool="review.stamp" />
      <InkCommand id="review.suggest" />
    </InkToolbar>
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  import {
    createCommandButton,
    createToolbar,
    createToolButton,
    createViewer,
    redactAreaTool,
  } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  import { review } from './review-plugin'


  const viewer = createViewer(el, {
    source: file,
    assets,
    tools: [redactAreaTool()],
    plugins: [review()],
  })


  const tools = createToolbar()
  tools.append(
    createToolButton(viewer, 'redact-area'),
    createToolButton(viewer, 'review.stamp'),
    createCommandButton(viewer, 'review.suggest')
  )
  viewer.element.prepend(tools)
  ```

A plugin’s decorations and page layers apply to every document without being placed.

## Command buttons

`InkCommand` (`createCommandButton` in plain DOM) renders a button with the command’s status text beside it:

* The button is named by the command’s label, a string or a function that returns one. See [Translations](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/translations/#labels-you-supply). It shows the command’s icon, or the label as text when the command has none.
* It is disabled until a document is ready, unless the plugin sets its own condition.
* While the command runs, the button keeps focus and carries `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-disabled="true"`, and pressing it does nothing. An async command stays busy until its promise settles, so a double click runs it once.
* The status, a short progress or result message such as “4 suggestions”, sits in a live region, so screen readers announce it.

`InkCommand` takes `asChild` (`as-child` in Vue, the `child` snippet in Svelte) to render your own element, as [Toolbars](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/toolbars/#rendering-your-own-element) describes. Its slot, render prop or snippet receives `{ label, busy }`.

### Your own control

To build a control of your own, `useCommand(id)` returns `run`, `enabled`, `busy`, `status`, `label` and `icon`. In Vue they are refs, in React plain values, and in Svelte getters on the returned object, so read them through it rather than destructure. `run` never rejects and does nothing while the command is disabled or busy.

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { useCommand } from '@inkbar/vue'


  const suggest = useCommand('review.suggest')
  </script>


  <template>
    <button type="button" :disabled="!suggest.enabled.value" @click="suggest.run()">
      {{ suggest.busy.value ? 'Checking…' : suggest.label.value }}
    </button>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import { useCommand } from '@inkbar/react'


  export function SuggestButton() {
    const suggest = useCommand('review.suggest')
    return (
      <button type="button" disabled={!suggest.enabled} onClick={() => void suggest.run()}>
        {suggest.busy ? 'Checking…' : suggest.label}
      </button>
    )
  }
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import { useCommand } from '@inkbar/svelte'


    const suggest = useCommand('review.suggest')
  </script>


  <button type="button" disabled={!suggest.enabled} onclick={() => suggest.run()}>
    {suggest.busy ? 'Checking…' : suggest.label}
  </button>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  `viewer.commands.get(id)` returns the command, or `undefined`. Its `enabled`, `busy` and `status` are readables. `commandLabel(command)` reads its label, a string or the result of a label function. It reads the label once, so read it again when `viewer.messages` changes:

  ```ts
  import { commandLabel } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


  const suggest = viewer.commands.get('review.suggest')
  if (suggest) {
    const label = () => (button.textContent = commandLabel(suggest))
    label()
    viewer.messages.subscribe(label)
    suggest.enabled.subscribe((on) => (button.disabled = !on))
    button.addEventListener('click', () => void suggest.run())
  }
  ```

Call `useCommand` inside `InkRoot`. Announce `status` yourself if your control shows it, for example in an element with `role="status"`.

## Plugin tools

A plugin tool’s id is `<plugin>.<id>`, so tool `stamp` of plugin `review` is `review.stamp`. Pass that id to `InkToolButton` (`createToolButton` in plain DOM). The tool needs no entry in `tools`. The button takes the tool’s own label and icon; pass `label` to change the name.

## Loading and saving records

A plugin can keep records of its own, such as suggestions, in a store that each open document gets. Inkbar keeps no plugin data. To load and save its records, give it two functions:

* `initial(doc)` returns the records a document opens with. It runs once for each document that opens.
* `onChange(list, change)` runs after every change, with the whole list as it now stands.

Pass them in the plugin’s `records` option, under the name of the plugin’s records. The plugin’s docs give the names; the review plugin calls its records `suggestions`:

```ts
const plugins = [
  review({
    records: {
      suggestions: {
        initial: (doc) => savedSuggestions.get(doc.key) ?? [],
        onChange: (list) => saveSuggestions(list),
      },
    },
  }),
]
```

`change` says what happened:

| `change.kind` | Carries                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `add`         | `record`, the record added                                                                                                                                     |
| `update`      | `id`, and `before` and `after`, the record on each side of the change                                                                                          |
| `remove`      | `record`, the record removed                                                                                                                                   |
| `replace`     | `reason` (`history` for undo and redo, `reset` when the plugin starts over), and `added`, `updated` and `removed`: the ids each replace touched, in list order |

Undo and redo arrive as one `replace` with reason `history`. Save the whole `list` then, or use the ids to save only what changed. The records are frozen: copy one before you change it.

## Reading records from your app

Your app can read and write a plugin’s records too, to show a count, a custom list or a summary. Name them `<plugin>.<name>`, as in `review.suggestions`. The handle follows the open document, and each write is one undo step, like the plugin’s own.

* Vue

  ```ts
  import { useRecords } from '@inkbar/vue'


  const { records, handle } = useRecords<Suggestion>('review.suggestions')
  // records.value is the live list; handle.value reads and writes it
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import { useRecords } from '@inkbar/react'


  const { records, handle } = useRecords<Suggestion>('review.suggestions')
  ```

* Svelte

  ```ts
  import { useRecords } from '@inkbar/svelte'


  const suggestions = useRecords<Suggestion>('review.suggestions')
  // Keep the object: it holds getters, and destructuring loses reactivity
  console.log(suggestions.records.length, suggestions.handle)
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  const suggestions = viewer.records<Suggestion>('review.suggestions')
  suggestions.list.subscribe((items) => render(items))
  suggestions.batch(() => {
    suggestions.update('s1', { status: 'accepted' })
    suggestions.remove('s2')
  })
  ```

The handle is the plugin’s own less `annotates`. `batch(fn)` makes several writes one undo step. In the framework packages the hook needs `InkRoot`, and until the plugins are set up `handle` is null and `records` is empty. An unknown key gives an empty handle that ignores writes and logs a warning once. To list the records as cards without writing the list yourself, see [Lists of records](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/sidebars/#lists-of-records).

## Undo with annotations

Plugin records share the viewer’s undo history with annotations. A plugin can make a record change and an annotation edit one step, so a single undo takes back both. Accepting a suggestion, for example, marks the suggestion accepted and adds a redaction; undo puts the suggestion back and removes the redaction.

* **Uncontrolled.** The document’s history covers both. `InkUndo` and `InkRedo` undo plugin steps like any other.
* **Controlled.** With history on (`history`, or `:history="true"` in Vue), each undo step also snapshots the plugin stores. Undo puts the records back at once and proposes the earlier annotation list to you, as [Controlled mode](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/controlled-mode/) describes. With history off there is no undo, for records or annotations.

## Server rendering

The framework packages set plugins up once `InkRoot` has mounted in the browser, never on the server. Until then:

* `InkCommand` renders its button disabled, with no label, and keeps it out of the accessibility tree (`aria-hidden`).
* `useCommand` returns a disabled command with an empty `label` and no `icon`. They fill in once the plugins are set up.
* Nothing `setup` creates, such as a store, exists yet.

`createViewer` runs in the browser only, so it sets plugins up as it creates the viewer.

## Errors

Once the plugins are set up, `InkCommand`, `useCommand` and `createCommandButton` log an `UnknownCommand` error to the console for an id no plugin registered. The error names the id and the command ids the plugins did register. The control stays disabled and hidden, as it is before setup, and the rest of the viewer keeps working.

Two plugins with the same id raise `DuplicatePlugin` when the viewer sets them up. A plugin whose own callbacks throw, such as a decoration or a page layer, has the error logged so the viewer and other plugins keep working. A command whose run fails logs the error and never rejects.

# Writing a plugin

> Write an Inkbar plugin with records, commands, marks and cards, once for every framework.

A plugin is a function of the plugin API that `definePlugin` turns into a factory. You write it against `@inkbar/core` and `@inkbar/core/dom`, and it runs in Vue, React, Svelte and `createViewer` alike. This page is for plugin authors. To add a plugin to your app, see [Plugins](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/plugins/).

## An example

This plugin suggests redactions. Suggest adds suggestions, the plugin’s own records, for the open document. Each open one is drawn as a mark over its text that opens a review card. Accept marks the suggestion accepted and adds a redaction linked to it, Dismiss sets it aside, and deleting that redaction puts the suggestion back up for review. Each of those is one undo step.

```ts
import type { Quad, Rect, RecordBase } from '@inkbar/core'
import { definePlugin } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


export interface Suggestion extends RecordBase {
  /** Page index, from 0. */
  page: number
  /** Where the text is, in PDF user space. */
  quads: Quad[]
  /** The box around `quads`, where the mark goes. */
  rect: Rect
  reason: string
  explanation?: string
  status: 'suggested' | 'accepted' | 'dismissed'
}


export const review = definePlugin('review', (plugin) => {
  // The open document's `review.suggestions` records; empty while none is open.
  const suggestions = plugin.records<Suggestion>('suggestions')


  // Accept adds a redaction linked to its suggestion. Deleting that redaction puts the
  // suggestion back, inside the delete's undo step.
  const redaction = suggestions.annotates('redact', {
    from: (s) => ({ page: s.page, quads: s.quads }),
    onRemoved: (s) => suggestions.update(s.id, { status: 'suggested' }),
  })


  plugin.command(
    'suggest', // placed as `review.suggest`
    'Suggest redactions',
    async ({ doc, signal }) => {
      const found = await findSuggestions(doc, { signal }) // your own code
      // Bound to this run's document: if another file opened meanwhile, this adds nothing.
      const added = suggestions.in(doc).addMissing(found)
      return added.length === 1 ? '1 suggestion' : `${added.length} suggestions`
    },
    { errorStatus: 'Could not check this document.' }
  )


  plugin
    .marks(suggestions, {
      where: (s) => s.status === 'suggested',
      rect: (s) => s.rect,
      label: (s) => `Suggested redaction: ${s.reason}`,
      className: 'review-mark',
      card: (s) => ({
        title: s.reason,
        label: 'Suggested redaction',
        ...(s.explanation && { body: s.explanation }),
        actions: {
          Accept: () => {
            suggestions.update(s.id, { status: 'accepted' })
            redaction.add(s)
          },
          Dismiss: () => suggestions.update(s.id, { status: 'dismissed' }),
        },
      }),
    })
    .scrollToFirst()
})
```

Core draws each mark as a bare `<button>`. Its look is your CSS:

```css
.review-mark {
  border: 2px dashed #c0392b;
  background: transparent;
  cursor: pointer;
}
```

The host passes `review()` in `plugins` and places the command with `<InkCommand id="review.suggest" />`. The sandbox’s [suggestions plugin](https://github.com/inkbar/inkbar/blob/main/apps/sandbox/src/plugin/suggestions.ts) is the full version, with sample data, a confidence colour on each mark and in its card, and a search of the page text.

## `definePlugin`

`definePlugin(id, setup)` checks the id and returns a factory. The id is lower-case kebab case: a letter, then letters, digits and hyphens (`review`, `pii-check`). Anything else throws `InkError('InvalidPluginId')`.

The id is the namespace for everything the plugin adds. Command `suggest` becomes `review.suggest`, tool `box` becomes `review.box` and records `suggestions` are keyed `review.suggestions`.

Calling the factory with the host’s options makes a plugin, and each call makes an independent one. `setup(plugin, options)` runs once per viewer with the plugin API and those options. It can return a function, which runs when the viewer is destroyed. Type your own options with `definePlugin<Options>(id, setup)`; every plugin also takes `records`, below.

## Records

`plugin.records<T>(name)` returns a handle on the open document’s records, keyed `<plugin>.<name>`. Each document that opens gets its own. The handle follows the open document, so keep it for the plugin’s lifetime: while no document is open it reads empty and its writes do nothing. A record is a plain object with a string `id`.

| Member                  | What it does                                                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `list`                  | A readable of the records, `[]` while no document is open. It emits when the records or the document change |
| `all()`                 | The records, in order                                                                                       |
| `find(id)`, `has(id)`   | The record or `undefined`, and whether it exists                                                            |
| `where(match)`          | The records that pass a function, or whose fields equal every field of an object                            |
| `add(record)`           | Adds a record and returns the stored copy. Throws `InkError('DuplicateId')` when the id is taken            |
| `addMissing(records)`   | Adds the records whose ids are not taken yet, and returns those it added                                    |
| `update(id, patch)`     | Merges `patch` into a record and returns it. An unknown id returns `undefined`                              |
| `remove(id)`            | Removes a record and returns it, or `undefined` for an unknown id                                           |
| `in(doc)`               | The same handle bound to `doc`, for commands                                                                |
| `annotates(type, spec)` | Links the records to annotations made from them. See [Linked annotations](#linked-annotations)              |
| `store()`               | The underlying record store, or `null`, for anything the handle lacks                                       |

Every records call is one undo step, and `plugin.batch` makes several one step. `addMissing` adds all its records in one step. `plugin.batch(fn)` is `history.batch`: everything `fn` changes, annotations and records alike, undoes together. `fn` must be synchronous.

### Loading and saving

Inkbar keeps no plugin data. The host hands each records name its `initial` and `onChange` through the factory’s `records` option, and `plugin.records(name)` picks them up by name, so the plugin passes nothing on:

```ts
review({ records: { suggestions: { initial, onChange } } })
```

* `initial(doc)` returns the records a document opens with, called once for each document.
* `onChange(list, change)` runs after every change, with the list as it now stands.

Options passed to `plugin.records(name, { initial, onChange })` win over the host’s.

## Commands

`plugin.command(id, label, run, options)` adds a command under `<plugin>.<id>` and returns it. `label` is a string or a function that returns one, so the button can follow your language; see [Translations](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/translations/). `run` receives:

* `doc`, the document open when the command started.
* `signal`, an `AbortSignal` that aborts when that document closes or another opens.

A string that `run` returns becomes the command’s status, which the command button announces; `undefined` clears it. A thrown error is logged and sets the status to the `errorStatus` option, “Something went wrong.” by default. `errorStatus` takes a string or a function. An abort sets no status. The status clears when the document changes. The other options are `icon` and `enabled`; without `enabled`, the command is enabled while a document is open and ready. The command is busy, and disabled, until `run` settles, so a double click runs it once.

Inside a command, write through `records.in(doc)`. A command often waits, for a request or for the page text, and the user can open another file meanwhile. A write through the plain handle after an `await` goes to whatever document is open then. `in(doc)` binds the handle to the run’s document, and once that document closes its writes do nothing, so a stale result goes nowhere.

## Marks

`plugin.marks(records, options)` draws a `<button>` over each record that passes `where`, on page `record.page` (from 0) at `rect(record)` in user space, in a page layer of its own. Records drawn as marks need a `page`.

* `rect(record)` and `label(record)`, the mark’s accessible name, are required.
* `where(record)` picks the records that get a mark. Default: all.
* `style(record)` returns inline styles, custom properties such as `--tint` included, `className` adds classes, and `attrs(record)` adds attributes such as `data-*` and `aria-*`. Core draws nothing else.
* `card(record)` opens a card when the mark is activated. See [Cards](#cards).
* `onActivate(record, mark)` runs when the mark is clicked, or activated with Enter or Space, for anything a card does not cover.

Each mark carries `data-record` with the record’s id and `data-plugin` with the plugin’s id. Marks redraw when the records change, undo and redo included, and when the page’s zoom or rotation changes. A mark that stays keeps its element, so focus and an open card survive a redraw. Presses and clicks on a mark go no further, so the active tool and listeners on the viewer’s root never see them. Marks are Tab stops after the page’s annotations.

`plugin.marks` returns a handle:

* `refresh()` redraws every mark, for marks that read state of your own that changed.
* `scrollToFirst()` scrolls the viewer to new marks. When records start to get a mark, added or changed to pass `where`, the viewer scrolls to the first of them in reading order, unless that one is in view already. Focus stays where it is, and the records a document opens with, undo and redo never scroll. It returns the handle, so you can chain it onto `plugin.marks(…)`.

## Cards

A card is a popover next to its mark, styled by `@inkbar/theme` like the viewer’s own popovers. `card(record)` returns:

* `title`, the card’s heading. A string or a function that returns one.
* `label`, the dialog’s accessible name, also a string or a function. Default: `title`.
* `meta`, an optional short line under the title, and `swatch`, an optional CSS colour for a dot before it.
* `body`, optional text under the meta line.
* `excerpt`, an optional line of context after the body, as `{ before, match, after }`. The `match` part is marked.
* `actions`, one button per entry, in order. Give an object, where each key is a button’s label, or an array of `{ label, run }`, where each `label` can be a function.
* `className`, classes added to the card.

The card is a `role="dialog"`. Its first action is the primary one and takes focus when the card opens. Each card action is one undo step. Actions must be synchronous: a write after an `await` falls outside the action’s undo step. After an action, the card re-renders if the mark stays. If the mark goes, the card closes and focus moves to the next of this `marks()` call’s marks, else the previous one, else the viewport. Escape or a press outside closes the card and returns focus to the mark.

The theme styles the card through these classes, which are yours to restyle:

| Class               | Element                      |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `.ink-card`         | The card                     |
| `.ink-card-title`   | The title                    |
| `.ink-card-meta`    | The meta line                |
| `.ink-card-swatch`  | The dot before the meta line |
| `.ink-card-body`    | The body                     |
| `.ink-card-excerpt` | The excerpt                  |
| `.ink-card-actions` | The row of action buttons    |

For anything richer, use `onActivate` with your own popover, as [Your own popovers](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/frameworks/plain-dom/#your-own-popovers) describes.

Records that pass a `marks` call’s `where` also appear in a record list, each as the same card with the same actions in the same undo step, so the cards you wrote for the marks give you a sidebar list with no further code. The app places it with `InkRecordList records="<plugin>.<name>"`, as [Sidebars](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/sidebars/#lists-of-records) shows. When a plugin has no `marks` call for these records, every record still lists, with its id as the title and no actions.

## Linked annotations

`records.annotates(type, spec)` links records to the annotations of `type` made from them. Call it in `setup`.

* `spec.from(record)` returns the annotation’s fields, without `type`. Without a `color`, the annotation gets the document’s default colour for its type.
* `spec.onRemoved(record, annotation)` runs once for each linked annotation the user removes, inside that edit’s undo step, so the record change undoes with the delete. It never runs on undo or redo.
* `spec.onChanged(record, annotation)` runs for each user update of a linked annotation, inside that edit’s undo step.

The returned link’s `add(record)` adds the annotation and stores the link in it at `custom.<plugin>.<records name>`, the record’s id: `custom.review.suggestions` in the example. `of(record)` returns the record’s linked annotations of this type, in document order. A record can have several. The link survives a Gloss export and import, so a host that saves both keeps them linked.

## Text and geometry

* `doc.pageText(page)` resolves to the page’s text items joined with single spaces. Most plugins that look for something start there.
* `quadsFromRect(rect)` from `@inkbar/core` returns the quads covering a rect, which text markup such as `redact` takes. `rectFromQuads(quads)` returns the box around them, where a mark goes.

## Going further

The `plugin` that `setup` receives is also the plugin’s context, with everything below. Use it for what the shorthands above do not cover: tools, decorations, page layers of your own, or stores without the handle.

A plugin can also be a plain object, `definePlugin({ id, setup(ctx) { … } })`, which checks the id and returns the plugin itself. The host passes it as it is, without a call.

### The context

| Member                       | What it does                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                         | The plugin’s id                                                                                                                       |
| `document`                   | A readable of the open `InkDocument`, or `null`                                                                                       |
| `history.batch(fn)`          | Makes everything `fn` changes, annotations and records alike, one undo step                                                           |
| `activated`                  | A readable of the activated annotation’s id, or `null`                                                                                |
| `setActivated(id)`           | Activates an annotation, or clears the activation with `null`. An id not in the open document is ignored                              |
| `root`                       | A readable of the viewport’s scroll container, or `null` while none is mounted                                                        |
| `commands.add(spec)`         | Adds a command and returns it                                                                                                         |
| `tools.add(tool)`            | Adds a tool                                                                                                                           |
| `decorate(fn)`               | Adds `data`, `classes` and a `description` to annotation elements                                                                     |
| `redecorate()`               | Runs every decoration again                                                                                                           |
| `store(name, options)`       | A readable of the record store for the open document, or `null`                                                                       |
| `storage`                    | Settings kept between visits under `plugin.<id>.`, in the root’s [storage](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/storage/#in-a-plugin)        |
| `onDocument(fn)`             | Runs `fn(doc)` for each document that opens. The function it returns runs when that document closes                                   |
| `onAnnotationEdit(fn)`       | Runs `fn(edit)` for every user add, update and remove of an annotation, inside that edit’s undo step                                  |
| `layer(spec)`                | Adds a page layer and returns a handle with `invalidate(page?)`                                                                       |
| `scrollTo(page, rect, opts)` | Scrolls the viewer so `rect`, in user space on `page`, is in view. `opts.behavior` is a `ScrollBehavior`. Moves no focus              |
| `search`                     | The viewer’s search state and actions, shared with the find bar. See [Search](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/search/)                  |
| `onPress(fn)`                | Runs `fn(press)` for a press on a page that nothing in Inkbar acted on. Returns a function that stops listening                       |
| `onLongPress(fn)`            | Runs `fn(press)` when a touch or pen is held still on a page that nothing in Inkbar acted on. Returns a function that stops listening |

A readable has `get()` and `subscribe(fn)`, which returns a function that stops it. `writable` from `@inkbar/core` makes one you can `set`.

### `commands.add`

`ctx.commands.add(spec)` takes:

* `id`, namespaced to `<plugin>.<id>`.
* `label`, which names the command’s button. It is required: an empty label throws `InkError('InvalidCommandLabel')`.
* `icon`, an optional icon node such as one from `@inkbar/icons`. Without one, the button shows the label as text.
* `enabled`, an optional readable of a boolean. Without it, the command is enabled while a document is open and ready.
* `status`, an optional readable of a short progress or result message. The command button announces it in a live region.
* `run()`, which may return a promise.

The returned command has `id`, `label`, `icon` and three readables: `enabled`, `busy` and `status`. It is busy from `run()` until the promise settles, and disabled while busy, so a double click runs it once. `command.run()` does nothing while the command is busy or disabled, and never rejects. A failure is logged. One caused by the document closing during the run (`DocumentDestroyed`) is dropped silently. Check `ctx.document.get()` after each `await`, so results for a closed document go nowhere. `plugin.command` does this for you through `run`’s `doc` and `signal`.

### Record stores

`ctx.store(name, options)` asks for a store keyed `<plugin>.<name>`. Each document that opens gets a fresh one, and the readable holds `null` while no document is open. Read it with `get()` when you need it rather than keep the store.

Inkbar keeps no plugin data. Accept `initial` and `onChange` from the host and pass them on:

* `initial(doc)` returns the records a document opens with, called once for each document.
* `onChange(list, change)` runs after every change, with the list as it now stands.

A store holds plain records, each with a string `id`:

| Member                     | What it does                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `key`                      | `<plugin>.<name>`                                                                                              |
| `list`                     | A readable of the records, in order                                                                            |
| `get(id)`                  | The record, or `undefined`                                                                                     |
| `add(record)`              | Adds a record and returns the stored copy. Throws `InkError('DuplicateId')` when the id is taken               |
| `update(id, patch)`        | Merges `patch` into a record and returns it. The id cannot change. An unknown id returns `undefined`           |
| `remove(id)`               | Removes a record and returns it, or `undefined` for an unknown id                                              |
| `replaceAll(list, reason)` | Replaces every record. Pass `'reset'` to start over: earlier undo steps no longer restore this store’s records |
| `on('change', fn)`         | Calls `fn(change)` after every change and returns a function that stops it                                     |

Records are stored as frozen copies, so the object you pass to `add` stays yours and a stored record never changes under you. Change one with `update`.

A change is one of `add` (with `record`), `update` (`id`, `before` and `after`), `remove` (`record`) or `replace`. A `replace` has a `reason`, `history` for undo and redo or `reset`, and the ids it `added`, `updated` and `removed`.

### One undo step

The stores you get from `ctx.store` join the viewer’s undo history. On its own each change is one step. To make several changes one step, annotations included, wrap them in `ctx.history.batch(fn)`, which `plugin.batch` calls. `fn` must be synchronous: changes made after an `await` inside it are not part of the batch.

`ctx.onAnnotationEdit(fn)` runs inside the user’s edit, so a record change made there undoes with the edit. It receives `add` (`annotation`), `update` (`id`, `before`, `after`) and `remove` (`annotation`, and `removed`: it and the replies removed with it). It never runs for undo and redo, which restore your records themselves. `annotates` builds on this. By hand, this puts a suggestion back up for review when the user deletes the redaction that accepted it:

```ts
ctx.onAnnotationEdit((edit) => {
  const store = suggestions.get()
  if (edit.kind !== 'remove' || !store) return
  for (const a of edit.removed) {
    const id = (a.custom?.review as { suggestionId?: string } | undefined)?.suggestionId
    if (id && store.get(id)?.status === 'accepted')
      store.update(id, { status: 'suggested' })
  }
})
```

The same works in controlled mode, where the host owns the annotation list.

### Page layers

`ctx.layer(spec)` adds a layer to every mounted page, above the annotations. Each page gets its own element, `div.ink-plugin-layer[data-plugin="<id>"]`, covering the page.

* `render(el, page, transform)` draws into `el`. It runs when the page mounts, whenever the page’s zoom or rotation changes, and when you call `invalidate`.
* `destroy(el, page)` is optional and runs when the page unmounts.

The handle’s `invalidate(page)` redraws one page, or every mounted page without an argument. A layer added after pages have mounted, from `onDocument` say, appears on them at once.

Keep your geometry in PDF user space: points, origin bottom-left, before the page’s `/Rotate`, as annotations are. `transform`, a `PageTransform`, is the only conversion you need:

* `toCssRect(rect)` returns `{ left, top, width, height }` in CSS pixels from the page’s top-left corner.
* `toCss(point)`, `toCssQuad(quad)` and `toCssLength(points)` convert a point, a quad or a length.
* `fromCss(point)`, `fromCssRect(cssRect)` and `fromCssLength(px)` go the other way.
* `cssWidth`, `cssHeight`, `zoom` and `rotation` describe the page as drawn.

### Presses

`ctx.onPress(fn)` and `ctx.onLongPress(fn)` tell you about a press on a page that nothing in Inkbar acted on. Listeners are removed when the plugin is torn down.

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


export const pressLog = definePlugin('press-log', (plugin) => {
  plugin.onPress(({ page, point, pointerType }) => {
    console.log('press', page, point, pointerType)
  })
  plugin.onLongPress(({ page, point }) => {
    console.log('long press', page, point)
  })
})
```

The payload is a `PagePress`: `page` is a zero-based index, `point` is in user space on that page, and `pointerType` is `'mouse'`, `'touch'` or `'pen'`.

A press is a pointer going down and up on a page without moving more than a few pixels. A mouse click is a press. A touch or pen held still for about half a second is a long press instead. It fires while the finger is still down, and the release reports nothing more. A mouse never long-presses. A touch that becomes part of a pinch before a long press fires is neither, and so is one that starts a scroll.

Both fire only under the text and rectangle select tools; any other tool owns every press. They also stay quiet when something else took the press: an annotation, a resize handle, a link, a form field, a mark or a text editor. A press that commits an open text editor or closes a popover reports nothing either. Inkbar leaves the browser’s own long-press behaviour alone, so text selection and context menus still work.

### Marks and the keyboard

A mark is anything you put in a layer that the user can press or focus.

* The layer lets presses through to the page and the tools underneath. The elements you put straight into it take presses back (`pointer-events: auto`), with or without `@inkbar/theme`. That rule has no specificity, so a rule of yours such as `pointer-events: none` on a mark wins.
* The viewer’s tools leave presses and keys on your marks alone. They still bubble up to the viewer’s root, so stop propagation if listeners there should not see them. `plugin.marks` stops them for you.
* A focusable mark is a Tab stop after the page’s annotations, in DOM order. Use a `<button>`: it gets Enter and Space as a click.
* Escape is yours to handle. A card opened with `createPopover`, as in [Your own popovers](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/frameworks/plain-dom/#your-own-popovers), closes on Escape and `createFocusReturn` sends focus back to the mark.

Replacing every mark on each render drops focus when a mark redraws. To keep it, reuse the marks that stay and only move them, as `plugin.marks` does.

### Tools and decorations

`ctx.tools.add(tool)` adds a tool under `<plugin>.<id>`. A tool has an `id`, a `cursor`, `activate(toolCtx)` and `deactivate()`, and optional `label`, `icon`, `kind` (`'sticky'`, the default, or `'one-shot'`), `claimsTouch` and pointer and key handlers. `toolCtx` gives it the annotation `store`, the `viewport` and more. The press handlers receive the page `hit`, whose `user` is the point in user space. Set `claimsTouch: true` to receive one-finger drags; the host then gives up one-finger scrolling over the document while the tool is active, and two fingers still scroll and zoom.

```ts
import type { PageHit, ToolContext } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


class BoxTool {
  id = 'box' // placed as `review.box`
  label = 'Box'
  cursor = 'crosshair'
  #ctx: ToolContext | null = null


  activate(ctx: ToolContext) {
    this.#ctx = ctx
  }
  deactivate() {
    this.#ctx = null
  }
  onPointerDown(e: PointerEvent, hit: PageHit | undefined, annotationId?: string) {
    if (!this.#ctx || !hit || annotationId) return
    const { x, y } = hit.user
    const a = this.#ctx.store.add({
      type: 'square',
      page: hit.page,
      rect: { x: x - 20, y: y - 20, width: 40, height: 40 },
    })
    this.#ctx.store.select([a.id])
  }
}


ctx.tools.add(new BoxTool())
```

The host places it with a tool button (`tool="review.box"`), which shows the tool’s own `label` and `icon`. It joins the viewer’s tools on its own, so the host leaves it out of `tools`. Its methods run on your own object, so inside them `this.id` is the id you gave (`box`), and a class instance keeps its `#private` fields.

`ctx.decorate(fn)` works like the host’s `decorateAnnotation`, which [Plain DOM](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/frameworks/plain-dom/#your-own-chrome) describes. Decorations apply after the host’s own and earlier plugins’, and the earlier ones win on a data key or description. They re-apply when the annotations change. Call `ctx.redecorate()` when one reads state of your own that changed.

### Publishing a plugin

A plugin you publish lists `@inkbar/core` under `peerDependencies`, so the app and every plugin share one copy. Add it under `devDependencies` too, for your own build and tests. Never list it under `dependencies`: a second copy would give your plugin its own `InkError` and `Readable` classes.

```json
{
  "name": "@acme/inkbar-review",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "peerDependencies": {
    "@inkbar/core": "^0.14.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@inkbar/core": "^0.14.0"
  }
}
```

The peer range says which Inkbar versions your plugin works with, and the package manager warns an app that installs it next to another. Import `definePlugin` from `@inkbar/core/dom`, and every type with `import type`, so the types add nothing to your bundle. Every type reachable from `InkPlugin`, `PluginContext`, `PluginApi` and `PluginOptions` is exported from `@inkbar/core` or `@inkbar/core/dom`, and Inkbar’s tests keep it that way. Export the factory your users call:

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


export const review = definePlugin('review', (plugin) => {
  // …
})
```

### Things to know

* The framework packages run `setup` once the viewer has mounted in the browser, never during server rendering. Until then the plugin’s commands are disabled, and anything `setup` creates, such as a store, does not exist yet.
* A layer’s `destroy` can run after the document’s stores have closed, so check `store.get()` for `null` there.
* An error thrown from your decoration, a layer’s `render` or `destroy`, or an `onDocument` callback is logged, so one plugin cannot break the viewer or the others.

### Errors

| Code                  | When                                                                                       |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `InvalidPluginId`     | `definePlugin` gets an id that is not lower-case kebab case                                |
| `DuplicatePlugin`     | Two plugins with the same id are passed to one viewer                                      |
| `InvalidCommandLabel` | `commands.add` gets an empty label                                                         |
| `DuplicateId`         | A command, tool or store name is taken within the plugin, or `add` gets a record id in use |
| `UnknownCommand`      | The host places a command id that no plugin registered. Logged, not thrown                 |

Each is an `InkError` from `@inkbar/core`, with the code on `error.code`.

# Saving

> Write annotations and form values into the PDF with @inkbar/engine, so Download, Print and doc.save() give the file as it looks on screen.

Inkbar writes a session’s annotations and changed form values into the PDF. Download, Print and `doc.save()` then give a file that looks as it does on screen, and other programs can read what was added. Open that file in Inkbar again and its annotations come back ready to edit.

Saving is opt-in. It needs `@inkbar/engine`, a build of PDFium that runs in the browser. The same engine [applies redactions](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/redaction/). Without it, Download and Print give the file as it was opened, and redaction marks cannot be applied.

## Turn it on

Install the engine:

```sh
pnpm add @inkbar/engine
```

Then pass a function that imports it as `engine`:

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  const engine = () => import('@inkbar/engine')
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot :src="url" :assets="assets" :engine="engine">
      <!-- … -->
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  const engine = () => import('@inkbar/engine')


  <InkRoot src={url} assets={assets} engine={engine}>
    {/* … */}
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    const engine = () => import('@inkbar/engine')
  </script>


  <InkRoot src={url} {assets} {engine}>
    <!-- … -->
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  const viewer = createViewer(el, {
    source,
    assets,
    engine: () => import('@inkbar/engine'),
  })
  ```

The download and print buttons, Ctrl or Cmd+S and Ctrl or Cmd+P then hand over the file with the session’s changes written into it. `doc.save()` resolves with the same bytes.

Inkbar loads the engine on the first save that has changes, or the first apply of redactions. A visit that does neither never loads it, and a save with no changes gives the bytes the file was opened from. The engine’s binary is 2.9 MB gzipped. A bundler picks up its wasm and worker from the package, so there is nothing to set up. To serve those files from a path of your own, see the [`@inkbar/engine` README](https://github.com/inkbar/inkbar/tree/main/packages/engine#serving-the-files).

Inkbar reads `engine` when a document opens. Without it, `doc.save()` rejects with `EngineUnavailable` once there are changes. With or without it, `doc.getData()` gives the bytes the file was opened from.

`doc.changed` is a readable that is true while the session differs from the file: its annotations from those it opened with, or a form value from the file’s. The file’s values are the ones the form holds when `ready` resolves. A value you set after that is a change, and so is one you pass at open.

### Opening documents yourself

A host that calls `openDocument` itself passes one more option, `pictures`. In a browser, `savePictures(document)` from `@inkbar/core/dom` supplies it. `createViewer` and the framework packages pass it for you.

```ts
import { openDocument } from '@inkbar/core'
import { savePictures } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


const doc = await openDocument(file, {
  assets,
  engine: () => import('@inkbar/engine'),
  pictures: savePictures(document),
})
```

`pictures` gives a save three things from the browser: a picture of each line of text the standard fonts cannot set, a PNG copy of an image that is neither PNG nor JPEG, and the text widths the screen uses. Without it, a save lays text out with the standard fonts’ own widths, so a line can break at a different word in the file than on screen. A text box with Chinese, Arabic or emoji text then fails the save with `SaveFailed`, and so does a stamp whose image is WebP.

## What goes into the file

* Each annotation becomes a standard PDF annotation that other programs can list, select and delete. A highlight is a Highlight, a note a Text annotation, a text box a FreeText and a drawing an Ink annotation. A loupe or a mask becomes a Stamp. A comment goes in the annotation’s contents, and replies are saved as replies.
* Each annotation’s look is drawn from the same description the screen uses, so it matches what you see in Inkbar, apart from [the differences below](#where-the-saved-file-differs-from-the-screen).
* Changed form values. Fields you did not change keep the look they came with.
* A redaction mark becomes a Redact annotation. A save does not apply it.

Caution

Saving does not redact. The text and images under a redaction mark are still in the saved file, and anyone can copy them. Applying the marks removes them: see [Redaction](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/redaction/).

An encrypted file keeps its password. With `engine`, the open document holds the password until it closes, because a save opens the file again in the engine.

### Signed files

A file with a digital signature is saved by appending the changes after the signed bytes, so the signature still verifies. Other viewers report that the file changed after signing. Any other file is rewritten.

Appending keeps the earlier versions of a signed file inside it. If you delete or edit an annotation that an earlier Inkbar save wrote into a signed file, a reader can still recover the old one from the earlier version. A rewrite drops it.

### Loupes

A saved loupe holds a copy of its whole page’s content, fonts and images included, and shows the part under the lens. If you redact that page later in another tool, the original content stays in the file inside the loupe. When Inkbar [applies redactions](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/redaction/), every loupe it writes gets a copy of the redacted page. A loupe that stays locked keeps its old copy, and the apply then fails ([the limits](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/redaction/#limits) say what to do). On a page with large images the copy also adds to the file’s size.

## Opening a saved file

Annotations Inkbar saved come back as session annotations, with the same ids, ready to edit. Saving again replaces them, so each one is in the file once. They are not an undo step and do not count as a change.

They arrive a moment after `ready`, as one `replace` change with `reason: 'file'`. Until then the file’s copy shows, locked. A signature saved on a signature field comes back on the field, and the field shows as signed.

In [controlled mode](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/controlled-mode/), `onChange` proposes them once, with `reason: 'file'`: your list with the saved annotations added. Apply that proposal as you apply any other, by pushing the list back. Until you push a list, the viewer does not show the saved annotations, and each save still keeps them in the file. The framework packages’ undo history takes your answer as its starting point, so undo does not remove them.

Some annotations stay locked:

* Annotations made by other programs.
* An annotation Inkbar saved that another program has since moved, edited, replied to or given a pop-up window. Inkbar’s own replies to a note that stays locked stay locked with it.
* Inkbar’s own annotations in an encrypted file.

## Where the saved file differs from the screen

* Text with characters outside the standard fonts, such as Chinese, Arabic or emoji, is saved as a picture of the line, at four pixels per point. It blurs at high zoom and cannot be selected. The annotation’s contents keep the text.
* The standard fonts (Helvetica, Times and Courier) are not embedded, so each viewer draws them with its own equivalent. Widths match, and letter shapes can differ slightly.
* A note’s drop shadow is not saved.
* A loupe in the saved file magnifies the page’s content only. It leaves out the annotations and form fields under it.
* Form fields look as the engine draws them, which can differ from how Inkbar draws them on screen.
* Another viewer may redraw an annotation its user edits there.
* The file grows a little each time it is saved and opened again: about 1.5 KB for a file with eighteen annotations. Saving several times in one session does not add to it.

XFA forms are not supported.

## When a save fails

When the engine cannot be loaded or cannot write the file, `doc.save()` rejects with `SaveFailed`:

* `details.stage` is `'engine'` when the engine could not be loaded or started, as when offline.
* `details.stage` is `'write'` when the engine could not open or write this file.
* `details.annotation` holds an annotation’s id when that annotation is the cause.

Download and Print then hand over nothing. The viewer says why in its message box, and your error handler (`onError`, or the `error` event in Vue) hears the error.

While a copy is being written, the download and print buttons show they are busy, and another press does nothing. Inkbar keeps the written copy until the next change, so Print after Download does not write the file twice.

The three messages are `saveFailed`, `saveUnavailable` and `preparingFile`, in the `viewer` group. [Translations](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/translations/) shows how to change them.

## Without the engine

You can still keep a session without writing into the PDF. Store the annotations and form values as JSON in your own backend and import them on the next open: [Annotations](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/annotations/#saving-annotations) and [Forms](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/forms/#save-values-as-gloss) show how.

# Storage

> Choose where Inkbar keeps saved signatures, sidebar widths and plugin settings between visits, from memory to localStorage to your own server.

Inkbar keeps a few small things between visits: saved signatures, sidebar widths and plugin settings. Your app decides where they go. Inkbar never touches `localStorage`, cookies or the network unless the store you pass does.

## Passing a store

Pass `storage` to the root. Without it, everything lasts until the page reloads.

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { createLocalStorage } from '@inkbar/core'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/vue'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  defineProps<{ file: File }>()


  const storage = createLocalStorage('my-app')
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot :src="file" :assets="assets" :storage="storage">
      <InkViewport />
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import { createLocalStorage } from '@inkbar/core'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/react'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  const storage = createLocalStorage('my-app')


  export function Viewer({ file }: { file: File }) {
    return (
      <InkRoot src={file} assets={assets} storage={storage}>
        <InkViewport />
      </InkRoot>
    )
  }
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import { createLocalStorage } from '@inkbar/core'
    import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


    let { file }: { file: File } = $props()


    const storage = createLocalStorage('my-app')
  </script>


  <InkRoot src={file} {assets} {storage}>
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  import { createLocalStorage } from '@inkbar/core'
  import { createViewer } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  const viewer = createViewer(el, {
    source: file,
    assets,
    storage: createLocalStorage('my-app'),
  })
  ```

The root reads `storage` once, when it is created. Signatures, sidebars inside the root and plugins all use it.

## The stores Inkbar ships

`@inkbar/core` has two:

* `createMemoryStorage(initial?)` is the default. It forgets everything on reload. Pass `initial`, an object of keys and values, to start it with something in it.
* `createLocalStorage(prefix = 'inkbar')` writes JSON to `localStorage` under `<prefix>:<key>`. It reads `localStorage` on every call, so a change made in another tab shows. Where the browser blocks storage, as some private windows do, or there’s no `localStorage` at all, as during server rendering, it keeps values in memory for the page’s life. When storage is full, `set` rejects with an `Error` whose `cause` is the browser’s, and the old value stays.

Give each app its own prefix, so two apps on one origin keep their values apart. Key it by user too when people share a browser, since a saved signature belongs to one person.

## Writing your own

A store has three methods. Each may answer straight away or return a promise, and every value is JSON:

```ts
interface InkStorage {
  get(key: string): unknown | Promise<unknown> // undefined when there is nothing
  set(key: string, value: unknown): void | Promise<void>
  remove(key: string): void | Promise<void>
}
```

This one keeps everything on your server:

```ts
import type { InkStorage } from '@inkbar/core'


const prefs = (key: string) => `/api/prefs/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`


export const storage: InkStorage = {
  get: async (key) => {
    const res = await fetch(prefs(key))
    return res.ok ? res.json() : undefined
  },
  set: async (key, value) => {
    const res = await fetch(prefs(key), {
      method: 'PUT',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(value),
    })
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Saving ${key} failed: ${res.status}`)
  },
  remove: async (key) => {
    await fetch(prefs(key), { method: 'DELETE' })
  },
}
```

Reject from `set` when a save fails. The signature dialog then tells the person their signature was not saved.

The same three methods fit a Redux or Pinia store, IndexedDB or anything else your app already keeps state in.

### Answering straight away

A store that answers straight away, as the memory and `localStorage` stores do, lets a sidebar take its saved width before it first paints. A store that returns promises works too, but the sidebar shows its default width first and moves to the saved one when it arrives. To avoid that jump with a server store, load the values with the page and answer `get` from them.

## The keys Inkbar uses

| Key                    | Value                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `signatures`           | An array of [signature templates](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/signatures/#where-signatures-are-kept) |
| `sidebar.<name>.width` | A [sidebar’s width](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/sidebars/#width), a number in CSS pixels             |
| `plugin.<id>.<key>`    | Whatever a plugin keeps                                                                                |

`scopeStorage(storage, prefix)` from `@inkbar/core` wraps a store so every key gains `<prefix>.`, which is how each plugin gets its own.

## In a plugin

A plugin gets `ctx.storage`, the root’s store scoped to `plugin.<id>`. A plugin with the id `review` that sets `panel` writes `plugin.review.panel`, and it can’t read or overwrite Inkbar’s keys or another plugin’s.

```ts
import { definePlugin } from '@inkbar/core/dom'


export const review = definePlugin({
  id: 'review',
  setup(ctx) {
    let showResolved = false
    void Promise.resolve(ctx.storage.get('showResolved')).then((saved) => {
      showResolved = saved === true
    })
    // Later, when the person changes the setting:
    // void ctx.storage.set('showResolved', true)
  },
})
```

`get` and `set` may return a promise, depending on the store, so wrap a read in `Promise.resolve` when you need the value.

Use `ctx.storage` for settings that outlast a document and a visit, such as a filter or a panel width. Use [`ctx.store(name)`](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/guides/writing-a-plugin/#record-stores) for records that belong to one document and undo with its edits.

Every plugin shares the page with your app, so scoping keeps plugins from clashing by accident. It doesn’t keep a plugin out on purpose.

# Theming

> Import the default stylesheet and restyle it with your own tokens and CSS.

`@inkbar/theme` holds the default styles for the Inkbar components: one stylesheet, no JavaScript.

Install it as the [Quickstart](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/quickstart/) shows.

Import the stylesheet once in your app:

```ts
import '@inkbar/theme/theme.css'
```

Every rule sits in `@layer inkbar` and inside `:where()`, so each selector has zero specificity. Your unlayered CSS overrides it without `!important`.

Annotations are the exception. Inkbar draws each one from its data and locks the paint, so a stylesheet cannot change an annotation’s fill, stroke or text. It can still hide, move or filter the annotation’s element.

## Layer order

Cascade layers win by order, whatever the specificity. The browser orders layers by first appearance, so if your stylesheet declares its own layers before this file loads, `inkbar` comes later and beats them. Declare `inkbar` first, at the top of your main stylesheet:

```css
@layer inkbar, utilities;
```

Put `inkbar` ahead of your own layer names, and your utility classes override the theme.

## Tokens

The stylesheet is compatible with shadcn token names. It reads `--background`, `--foreground`, `--muted`, `--muted-foreground`, `--border`, `--primary`, `--primary-foreground`, `--ring` and `--radius` when your page defines them, and uses its own values when it does not. Dark values apply under `prefers-color-scheme: dark` or inside a `.dark` ancestor. Add `.light` to the root or an ancestor to keep the light values, including inside a `.dark` ancestor.

Colour tokens must hold complete CSS colour values. Tokens written as bare HSL channels (`--muted: 210 40% 96%`) do not work. Write the full colour instead:

```css
--muted: hsl(210 40% 96%);
```

## Layout

The root and viewport fill their parent as a column, and the scroll area takes the remaining height. Give the parent a height and the document scrolls inside it.

## Toolbars

The theme gives each toolbar a background and padding and styles the controls in it. You decide where the toolbar sits and what separates it from the document. `--ink-control-size` and `--ink-icon-size` set the size of a toolbar’s controls and icons:

```css
.my-page-bar {
  --ink-control-size: 2rem;
  --ink-icon-size: 1rem;
  border-top: 1px solid var(--border);
}
```

## Your own controls

Two classes give your own controls the look of the built-in ones. Add `ink-select` to a `<select>` to give it the zoom select’s box and chevron. To put an icon in a field, wrap the input in `ink-input-group` and add an `ink-input-accessory` before it for an icon at the start, or after it for one at the end. The icon lets clicks through to the field, and the input makes room for it. The find bar and the search results field use this for their search icon.

```html
<select class="ink-select">
  …
</select>


<div class="ink-input-group">
  <span class="ink-input-accessory"><svg aria-hidden="true">…</svg></span>
  <input type="text" aria-label="Filter notes" />
</div>
```

## Annotation colours

The annotation colours have their own variables, such as `--ink-highlight` and `--ink-redact`. The theme declares them on the root element, so set yours there too:

```css
[data-ink-root] {
  --ink-highlight: #e4ff4a;
}
```

[Theme tokens](/pr-preview/pr-52/docs/reference/theme-tokens/) lists them all, along with the interface tokens.

# Translations

> Show Inkbar in your own language with the French and German sets, override single strings, switch language live, and translate the labels you supply.

Every string Inkbar shows comes from `messages`. English is the default. French and German ship with the library, and any other language is a set of strings you pass in.

## Why strings

`messages` is a plain object of strings and small functions. Inkbar asks nothing of your translation setup, so it works with whatever your app uses, or with nothing. The examples here call a generic `t(key, params)` where your own function goes.

A set is nested by feature area, such as `toolbar` and `find`. `messages` takes a partial set, and a key you leave out stays English.

## Override a few keys

Pass only what you want to change.

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/vue'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  defineProps<{ file: File }>()


  const messages = { toolbar: { find: 'Search this file' } }
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot :src="file" :assets="assets" :messages="messages">
      <InkViewport />
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/react'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  const messages = { toolbar: { find: 'Search this file' } }


  export function Viewer({ file }: { file: File }) {
    return (
      <InkRoot src={file} assets={assets} messages={messages}>
        <InkViewport />
      </InkRoot>
    )
  }
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


    let { file }: { file: File } = $props()


    const messages = { toolbar: { find: 'Search this file' } }
  </script>


  <InkRoot src={file} {assets} {messages}>
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  import { createViewer } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  const viewer = createViewer(el, {
    source: file,
    assets,
    messages: { toolbar: { find: 'Search this file' } },
  })
  ```

Passing `messages` again replaces the last value, so overrides do not pile up.

## French and German

Each language is its own entry point, so your bundler drops the ones you don’t import.

* Vue

  ```vue
  <script setup lang="ts">
  import { fr } from '@inkbar/core/locales/fr'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/vue'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  defineProps<{ file: File }>()
  </script>


  <template>
    <InkRoot :src="file" :assets="assets" :messages="fr">
      <InkViewport />
    </InkRoot>
  </template>
  ```

* React

  ```tsx
  import { fr } from '@inkbar/core/locales/fr'
  import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/react'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  export function Viewer({ file }: { file: File }) {
    return (
      <InkRoot src={file} assets={assets} messages={fr}>
        <InkViewport />
      </InkRoot>
    )
  }
  ```

* Svelte

  ```svelte
  <script lang="ts">
    import { fr } from '@inkbar/core/locales/fr'
    import { InkRoot, InkViewport } from '@inkbar/svelte'
    import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


    let { file }: { file: File } = $props()
  </script>


  <InkRoot src={file} {assets} messages={fr}>
    <InkViewport />
  </InkRoot>
  ```

* Plain DOM

  ```ts
  import { createViewer } from '@inkbar/core/dom'
  import { fr } from '@inkbar/core/locales/fr'
  import { assets } from 'virtual:inkbar-assets'


  const viewer = createViewer(el, { source: file, assets, messages: fr })
  ```

`de` comes from `@inkbar/core/locales/de`. To change a string in a shipped set, spread it: `messages: { ...fr, find: { ...fr.find, field: 'Chercher' } }`.

Both sets are drafts. If a string reads wrong to you, [open an issue on inkbar/inkbar](https://github.com/inkbar/inkbar/issues) with the key and the wording you would use.

## Messages with values

A message that takes values is a function of one params object. Call your own `t` from it:

```ts
import type { InkMessagesInput } from '@inkbar/core'


declare function t(key: string, params?: object): string


const messages: InkMessagesInput = {
  lang: 'es',
  find: {
    field: t('find.field'),
    count: ({ current, total }) => t('find.count', { current, total }),
  },
}
```

Plurals are your `t`’s job. It knows your language’s rules, so `find.count` returns “1 de 1” or “2 de 7” in the form your language needs.

To do the same by hand, use the two helpers from `@inkbar/core`. `template` fills `{name}` placeholders. `plural` picks a form by the language’s plural rule for one parameter, and `other` is the fallback:

```ts
import { plural, template } from '@inkbar/core'


const messages = {
  lang: 'en',
  search: {
    resultCount: plural('en', 'count', {
      one: '{count} result',
      other: '{count} results',
    }),
  },
  thumbnails: {
    page: template('en', 'Page {page}'),
  },
}
```

Both format numbers for the language you give them, so 1200 reads `1,200` in English and `1.200` in German. The shipped sets are built with them.

## Switching live
